outputs.L1:
(CNN) — The European Commission issued its ruling Wednesday in a landmark antitrust case against Intel, fining the computer-chip giant a record $1.45 billion for abusing its dominant position in the computer processing unit (CPU) market.

The ruling, which Intel plans to appeal, could have future implications for American companies accused of “jurisdiction shopping” to avoid unfavorable antitrust verdicts, says CNN’s Jim Boulden, who explains the fundamentals of the Intel case.

**The commission has imposed its largest fine ever. What were its reasons?**

The European Commission says Intel has abused its dominant market position in semiconductors for years. According to the commission, Intel systematically offered rebates to PC makers and retailers to keep computers using AMD chips off store shelves. AMD—another American company and Intel’s only competitor—first raised concerns in 2000.

**Why does the commission have the authority to impose such fines?**

EU law does not consider market dominance illegal in itself, but it permits regulators to fine a company that abuses its position as the largest player in a given market. The commission’s guidelines allow fines to be calculated as a percentage of profits. EU law is designed to “protect consumers,” and the antitrust office says consumers were harmed.

As Intel has pointed out, however, consumers did not initiate this case. AMD, a competitor, brought the complaint in Europe—as well as in Japan and South Korea—at a time when U.S. antitrust officials under President George W. Bush were unlikely to pursue a case on similar grounds.

The EU could have fined Intel, or any company, up to 10 percent of its global annual revenue, but chose instead to impose a smaller percentage based on revenue generated in the EU.

**Can Intel afford to pay the fine? What is the company’s current position?**

Intel reported first-quarter revenue of $7 billion, meaning it can readily afford the fine. Interestingly, the company has lost 4 percent of its market share to AMD so far this year.

**Intel says it will appeal. When is the appeal likely to be heard?**

A further appeal will take months. Intel already appealed a preliminary part of this ruling last year and lost. In the meantime, the European Commission may argue that Intel is continuing to abuse its position and could increase the fine during the appeals process, as it did with Microsoft.

**Intel is not the first technology company to face action from the European Commission. What about Microsoft?**

The antitrust unit has launched another round of investigations into Microsoft. The company has already paid its fine, and the EU continues to monitor its conduct in relation to previous matters.

**What kind of precedent does the Intel case set?**

The EU has fined many cartels and companies accused of abusing market power, but it rarely fines major American companies based on complaints from American competitors. For that reason, the case has attracted attention, particularly among critics who accuse American companies of “jurisdiction shopping” to secure a more favorable outcome.

The European Commission issued a decision Wednesday in a major antitrust case involving Intel, imposing a record $1.45 billion penalty on the computer-chip maker for misusing its powerful position in the market for central processing units, or CPUs.

Intel has said it intends to challenge the ruling. CNN’s Jim Boulden said the case could have broader consequences for U.S. firms accused of seeking out legal venues where they are more likely to win antitrust disputes.

Why did the commission impose such a large penalty?

According to the European Commission, Intel spent years taking advantage of its leading position in the semiconductor industry. Regulators said the company repeatedly offered rebates to computer manufacturers and retailers in order to prevent machines containing chips made by AMD from being sold. AMD, also a U.S. company and Intel’s only rival in that market, first raised concerns in 2000.

How is the commission able to levy fines like this?

Under European Union rules, simply being dominant in a market is not unlawful. However, a company can be punished if it exploits that dominance unfairly. The EU uses guidelines that allow fines to be calculated as a share of a company’s profits.

EU competition law is designed to safeguard consumers, and antitrust officials said consumers were harmed in this case. Intel, however, has emphasized that consumers were not the ones who brought the complaint. Instead, AMD pursued the matter in Europe, as well as in Japan and South Korea, at a time when U.S. antitrust authorities under President George W. Bush were not expected to bring a case on those grounds.

The EU could have based Intel’s penalty, or a penalty against any company, on as much as 10 percent of worldwide annual revenue. In this case, it chose a smaller percentage tied to revenue generated in Europe.

Can Intel pay the fine, and how is the company doing?

Intel reported revenue of $7 billion in the first quarter, so the fine is not expected to be financially unmanageable for the company. At the same time, AMD has gained ground: Intel has lost 4 percent of its market share to AMD so far this year.

When might Intel’s appeal be heard?

A further appeal is expected to take several months. Intel had already challenged an earlier, preliminary portion of the decision last year, but that appeal failed. During the appeals process, the European Commission can continue to argue that Intel is still abusing its market power and could raise the fine, as it previously did in Microsoft’s case.

Has the European Commission targeted other technology companies?

Yes. Microsoft has also faced action from the EU’s antitrust authorities. The commission has opened another series of investigations into Microsoft. The company has already paid its earlier fine, and EU regulators are continuing to monitor its conduct in relation to those previous issues.

What precedent does this case create?

The European Union has penalized many cartels and companies accused of abusing market power. However, it is unusual for it to fine major American corporations based on complaints brought by other American competitors. That makes the Intel case especially notable, particularly to critics who say some U.S. companies engage in “jurisdiction shopping” in search of a more favorable legal result.

## Intel’s $1.45 billion EU antitrust fine: A Q&A explainer

**Jim Boulden, CNN-style explainer:** The European Commission has hit Intel with a record antitrust fine — **€1.06 billion, about $1.45 billion at the time** — after concluding the chipmaker abused its dominant position in the computer processor market to keep rival AMD at bay.

### Q: What did the European Commission accuse Intel of doing?

**A:** EU regulators said Intel used its market power in computer chips — specifically **x86 central processing units**, the main processors used in most PCs — to unfairly squeeze out competition.

The Commission said Intel offered **rebates and payments** to major computer makers and retailers on the condition that they limit or delay the use of chips made by rival **Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD**.

In Brussels’ view, this wasn’t ordinary discounting. Regulators argued the deals were structured to make it commercially difficult for PC makers to choose AMD, even when AMD had competitive products.

### Q: Which companies were involved?

**A:** The Commission said Intel gave conditional rebates to major PC manufacturers including **Dell, HP, NEC and Lenovo**. It also said Intel made payments to **Media-Saturn**, a large European electronics retailer, to sell computers containing Intel chips rather than AMD chips.

The EU’s case centered on whether these arrangements effectively shut AMD out of key parts of the market.

### Q: Why was the fine so large?

**A:** The fine was meant to reflect both the seriousness and duration of the conduct. At the time, it was the **largest antitrust fine ever imposed by the European Commission on a single company**.

EU Competition Commissioner Neelie Kroes said the behavior harmed consumers by reducing choice and stifling innovation. The Commission’s argument was that if AMD was prevented from competing fairly, PC makers and consumers ultimately lost out.

### Q: What did Intel say in response?

**A:** Intel denied wrongdoing and said its practices were lawful, competitive and beneficial to customers. The company argued that it competed aggressively on price and performance, and that its rebates were legitimate discounts — not illegal exclusionary tactics.

Intel said it would **appeal** the decision.

### Q: What happens during an appeal?

**A:** Intel could challenge the Commission’s decision before the European courts. An appeal would focus on whether the Commission properly applied EU competition law and whether it had enough evidence to prove Intel’s conduct harmed competition.

Appeals in major EU antitrust cases can take years. Companies often argue that regulators misunderstood the market, overestimated their dominance, or failed to prove that the disputed conduct actually excluded competitors.

### Q: What role did AMD play?

**A:** AMD was Intel’s main rival in the x86 processor market and had long complained that Intel’s business practices prevented fair competition.

AMD’s complaints helped trigger regulatory scrutiny in Europe and elsewhere. The EU case essentially accepted AMD’s argument that Intel’s rebate arrangements and payments made it harder for AMD to win major contracts with PC manufacturers.

### Q: Was this only a European issue?

**A:** No. Intel had faced scrutiny in multiple jurisdictions, including investigations and legal disputes in the United States, Japan and South Korea. But the European Commission’s decision was especially significant because of the size of the fine and the EU’s willingness to take aggressive action against dominant technology companies.

### Q: How does this compare with Microsoft’s EU antitrust battles?

**A:** The comparison is natural. Microsoft had previously been fined heavily by the European Commission for abusing its dominance in software, including issues involving Windows, media software and interoperability with rival products.

Both cases involved major American technology companies accused of using dominance in one market to restrict competition. But the details differed:

- **Microsoft** was mainly about software bundling and interoperability.
- **Intel** was about rebates, payments and alleged exclusion of a hardware rival.
- In both cases, the EU framed its actions as protecting consumer choice and innovation.

### Q: Why does this matter for consumers?

**A:** Antitrust regulators argue that competition leads to lower prices, better products and more innovation. If a dominant company can prevent rivals from gaining market access, consumers may see fewer choices and slower technological progress.

In Intel’s case, the Commission said AMD was denied a fair chance to compete for major PC contracts — and that could have affected what computers were available and at what price.

### Q: What is the bigger takeaway?

**A:** The EU’s message was clear: even the biggest technology companies can offer discounts and compete hard, but they cannot use dominance to block rivals unfairly.

For Intel, the fine was a major legal and financial setback. For AMD, it was validation of years of complaints. And for the tech industry, it was another sign that Brussels was prepared to act forcefully when it believed market power was being abused.

# Q&A: The Basics of the EU Antitrust Case Against Intel

**BRUSSELS —** The European Union’s long-running antitrust case against Intel centers on whether the U.S. chipmaker used its dominant position in computer processors to unfairly squeeze out its main rival, Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD. At issue are rebates and payments Intel offered to major computer manufacturers and retailers during the 2000s.

Below is a question-and-answer guide to the case and why it mattered.

---

## What was the EU case against Intel about?

The European Commission accused Intel of abusing its dominant position in the market for x86 central processing units — the main chips used in most personal computers.

Regulators said Intel used financial incentives to discourage major PC makers from buying chips from AMD. The Commission argued that Intel’s conduct limited competition not by making better or cheaper products available, but by using its market power to make it financially unattractive for customers to deal with its rival.

Intel denied wrongdoing and argued that its discounts were legitimate competitive behavior that benefited customers.

---

## How large was the fine?

In 2009, the European Commission imposed a fine of **€1.06 billion**, then one of the largest antitrust penalties ever levied by the EU against a single company.

The fine reflected the Commission’s view that Intel’s conduct was serious, long-running and affected a strategically important technology market. Intel challenged the decision in European courts, and the litigation continued for years, including later rulings that scrutinized how the Commission assessed whether Intel’s rebates were capable of harming competition.

---

## What rebates did Intel give to PC makers?

The Commission said Intel offered rebates to major computer manufacturers on the condition that they bought all, or almost all, of their x86 chips from Intel.

The companies named in the case included major PC makers such as **Dell, Hewlett-Packard, NEC and Lenovo**. According to EU regulators, Intel’s rebates were structured in a way that made it costly for these manufacturers to shift meaningful business to AMD.

The case also involved payments to the German retailer **Media-Saturn**, which regulators said were aimed at ensuring the retailer sold only computers equipped with Intel chips.

---

## Why are rebates a problem? Aren’t discounts good for consumers?

Rebates and discounts are not automatically illegal. In many markets, they are a normal form of price competition and can lower costs for customers.

The EU’s concern was that Intel’s rebates were allegedly conditional on exclusivity or near-exclusivity. When a dominant company offers discounts that customers lose if they buy from a rival, regulators may view those rebates as exclusionary rather than merely price-cutting.

In simple terms, the question was not whether Intel charged lower prices. The question was whether Intel used its dominant position to prevent AMD from competing on the merits.

---

## What was the alleged consumer harm?

The European Commission argued that consumers may have been harmed even if they did not immediately see higher prices.

Regulators said that if AMD was blocked from gaining sales, the market could become less competitive over time. That could mean fewer choices, less innovation and potentially higher prices in the long run.

Intel argued that consumers benefited from strong competition, falling PC prices and rapid technological improvement during the relevant period. It also maintained that AMD remained a viable competitor and that customers chose Intel products for legitimate business and performance reasons.

---

## Why did the EU have jurisdiction over a U.S. company?

The EU can apply its competition rules to companies based outside Europe if their conduct affects competition in the European Economic Area.

Intel is an American company, but its chips were sold in computers throughout Europe. The Commission said the alleged practices affected the European market, giving EU regulators authority to investigate and impose penalties.

This principle is common in antitrust enforcement: a company’s headquarters do not shield it from regulation in markets where it sells products or where its conduct has significant effects.

---

## Did Intel’s finances affect the case?

Intel’s financial strength was relevant mainly because it helped explain why the company was considered dominant and why regulators believed its conduct could influence the market.

At the time, Intel was the world’s leading maker of PC processors, with substantial revenue, profit and market share. The Commission viewed that position as giving Intel the ability to shape the choices of PC manufacturers and retailers.

The size of the fine was also tied to factors such as the value of sales in the affected market, the gravity and duration of the alleged infringement, and deterrence. EU fines are intended not only to punish past conduct but also to discourage future violations.

---

## How does this compare with the EU’s earlier Microsoft case?

The Intel case followed another major EU antitrust action against a U.S. technology company: **Microsoft**.

In the Microsoft case, the European Commission found that Microsoft had abused its dominance in PC operating systems. The EU objected to practices including tying Windows Media Player to Windows and withholding interoperability information from competitors.

Both cases reflected the EU’s willingness to intervene in technology markets where it believed a dominant company was using its position to restrict competition. But the legal theories differed: Microsoft’s case focused on tying and interoperability, while Intel’s centered on rebates, exclusivity and alleged foreclosure of a chip rival.

---

## What is “jurisdiction shopping,” and how does it relate to this case?

“Jurisdiction shopping” refers to the idea that complainants may bring allegations to regulators in places where they believe enforcement is more likely, faster or tougher.

In global antitrust disputes, companies often complain to multiple authorities, including in the United States, Europe and Asia. Critics of aggressive enforcement sometimes argue that rivals use foreign regulators to gain leverage when they cannot win enough business in the marketplace.

Supporters of EU enforcement reject that characterization. They argue that competition authorities have a duty to investigate credible evidence of harm in their markets, regardless of where the companies are based or who files the complaint.

In Intel’s case, AMD had complained about Intel’s business practices in multiple jurisdictions. The EU maintained that its case was based on the effect of Intel’s conduct on European competition, not on favoring one company over another.

---

## Why did the case matter?

The Intel case became a landmark in the debate over how antitrust law should treat loyalty rebates by dominant firms.

For regulators, the case was about preventing a market leader from using financial incentives to shut out competitors. For Intel and many business groups, it raised concerns that ordinary discounting could be penalized if authorities misread competitive behavior.

The broader issue remains central to modern antitrust enforcement: how to distinguish hard competition that benefits consumers from exclusionary conduct that weakens competition over time.

The European Commission has fined U.S. chipmaker Intel a record **$1.45 billion** for abusing its dominant position in the computer processor market, marking one of the most significant antitrust actions ever taken by European regulators against an American technology company.

The ruling also adds to long-standing tensions between European regulators and major U.S. technology companies, many of which have faced investigations over competition, consumer protection and market dominance.

# Intel’s EU Antitrust Fine: What Happened, Why It Matters, and What Comes Next

## What did the European Commission fine Intel for?

The European Commission fined Intel for abusing its dominant position in the market for x86 central processing units — the chips used in most personal computers and servers.

The case centered on Intel’s conduct during the 2000s, when its main rival was AMD. The Commission alleged that Intel used its market power to restrict AMD’s ability to compete. The conduct included payments and commercial arrangements with major computer manufacturers and retailers that, according to the Commission, encouraged or required them to delay, cancel, or limit products using AMD processors.

In its original 2009 decision, the Commission imposed a fine of about €1.06 billion. After years of litigation, EU courts annulled part of that decision relating to certain rebate practices, but upheld findings concerning so-called “naked restrictions” — direct payments or incentives aimed at limiting AMD-based products. In 2023, the Commission re-imposed a reduced fine of about €376 million based on the upheld conduct.

## Why was the fine imposed?

The fine was imposed because the Commission concluded that Intel had abused a dominant market position, contrary to EU competition law.

Under Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, a company that holds a dominant position is not automatically breaking the law. However, it has a special responsibility not to use that power to distort competition.

The Commission’s concern was not simply that Intel competed aggressively. Price cuts, innovation, and better products are lawful and encouraged. The problem, according to the Commission, was that Intel’s arrangements were designed to exclude AMD from key sales channels and product launches rather than compete purely on the merits.

The Commission found that Intel’s behavior could reduce consumer choice, slow competition, and protect Intel’s position in the processor market.

## What exactly were the problematic practices?

The case involved two broad categories of conduct.

First, there were conditional rebates and payments to computer makers. The Commission argued that Intel offered financial incentives to companies such as Dell, HP, Lenovo, and NEC on the condition that they bought all or almost all of their x86 CPUs from Intel.

Second, there were “naked restrictions.” These were payments or incentives allegedly given to manufacturers to delay, cancel, or restrict the sale of computers containing AMD chips. This part of the case ultimately proved more durable in court.

The EU courts required a more rigorous economic analysis of the rebate allegations, and part of the original Commission decision was annulled. But the findings about direct restrictions on AMD-based products survived, leading to the reduced fine.

## Can Intel afford to pay the fine?

Yes. Intel is a large multinational semiconductor company, and a fine of several hundred million euros, while significant, is not existential for the company.

That does not mean the fine is trivial. It can affect earnings, cash flow, and investor perception, and it may come on top of legal costs and other business pressures. But compared with Intel’s historical revenues, assets, and access to capital, the fine is financially manageable.

Large companies in EU competition cases often either pay the fine, set aside accounting provisions, or provide financial guarantees while litigation continues. The exact financial treatment depends on the status of appeals and accounting rules.

## Does Intel have to pay immediately if it appeals?

An appeal does not automatically erase the obligation created by the Commission’s decision.

In EU competition cases, a company may challenge the Commission’s decision before the General Court of the European Union. If it loses there, it can appeal further to the Court of Justice of the European Union, but usually only on points of law.

During an appeal, the company may still be required to pay the fine or provide a bank guarantee. In some circumstances, it can seek interim relief to suspend payment, but that is difficult to obtain. The company must generally show urgency and serious risk of irreparable harm.

If Intel ultimately wins on appeal, the fine may be reduced or annulled, and amounts already paid may be returned with interest. If Intel loses, the fine stands, potentially with interest depending on the procedural posture.

## What happens during the appeal?

On appeal, the court reviews whether the Commission made legal errors, procedural errors, or manifest errors in its assessment of the facts and evidence.

The court may consider questions such as:

- Did Intel hold a dominant position in the relevant market?
- Did the Commission correctly define the market?
- Was the conduct capable of restricting competition?
- Did the Commission provide sufficient economic analysis?
- Was the fine calculated lawfully and proportionately?
- Were Intel’s rights of defense respected?

The Intel litigation has already had a major impact on how EU courts assess rebate schemes by dominant companies. The courts made clear that, when a dominant company argues that its rebates were not capable of foreclosing an equally efficient competitor, the Commission must seriously examine that argument.

## How is Microsoft relevant?

Microsoft is relevant mainly as a comparison and precedent, not because Microsoft was accused of wrongdoing in the Intel case.

The European Commission’s earlier antitrust actions against Microsoft were landmark cases in EU competition law. Microsoft was fined for abusing its dominant position in PC operating systems, including conduct related to interoperability information and tying Windows Media Player to Windows.

Those cases showed that the Commission was willing to take aggressive action against dominant technology companies, even very powerful U.S.-based firms. They also helped establish the EU as one of the world’s most active antitrust enforcers in technology markets.

Intel’s case belongs to the same broader tradition: EU regulators scrutinizing whether dominant technology companies use their position to shut out rivals rather than compete on the merits.

Microsoft is also relevant because Intel’s chips and Microsoft’s Windows operating system historically formed the “Wintel” ecosystem that dominated the PC market. The health of competition in PCs depended not only on software competition but also on hardware and processor competition. However, Microsoft was not the target of the Intel fine.

## Did the Commission “win” or “lose” the Intel case?

The answer is mixed.

The Commission did not fully preserve its original 2009 decision. A major part of the case involving conditional rebates was annulled after the courts found that the Commission had not sufficiently analyzed whether the rebates were capable of foreclosing competition.

However, the Commission did preserve important findings concerning Intel’s direct restrictions on AMD-based products. That allowed the Commission to re-impose a substantial, though much smaller, fine.

So the case was both a setback and a partial victory for the Commission. It lost a large part of the original fine but preserved the principle that dominant companies cannot pay customers or partners to suppress rival products.

## What precedent does the case set?

The Intel case sets several important precedents in EU antitrust law.

First, it confirms that dominant companies cannot use payments, exclusivity arrangements, or commercial pressure to block rivals from reaching customers.

Second, it raises the evidentiary bar for the Commission in cases involving loyalty rebates. The Commission must examine economic evidence when a company argues that its conduct was not capable of excluding an equally efficient competitor.

Third, it distinguishes between complex rebate schemes and more direct exclusionary conduct. Rebate systems may require detailed economic analysis, but direct payments to delay or cancel rival products are more plainly suspect.

Fourth, it reinforces the idea that EU competition law applies strongly to technology markets, where network effects, scale, and control over key supply channels can make foreclosure especially harmful.

Finally, the case serves as a warning to dominant firms: aggressive competition is lawful, but using market power to prevent customers or partners from dealing with rivals can lead to major penalties, even many years after the conduct occurred.

## Why does the case matter beyond Intel?

The Intel case matters because it affects how competition authorities approach powerful companies in fast-moving technology sectors.

Modern technology markets often depend on ecosystems: chips, operating systems, cloud infrastructure, app stores, devices, and distribution channels. A dominant company may be able to weaken rivals not only by cutting prices or improving products, but by controlling access to customers, manufacturers, retailers, or software platforms.

The Intel case shows that EU regulators and courts will look closely at whether business incentives are legitimate competition or exclusionary tactics. It also shows that the Commission must support major antitrust findings with careful evidence and economic reasoning.

For companies, the lesson is clear: dominance is not illegal, but exclusionary conduct can be. For regulators, the lesson is equally clear: even strong antitrust theories must be backed by rigorous analysis capable of surviving judicial review.
